newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-Strong dollar equals Buba rate rise?
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Strong dollar equals Buba rate rise?

text.p: By Ulrike Kastens, Economic Analyst at Trinkaus Capital Management in Duesseldorf

The Bundesbank has watched the US dollar rise against the D-mark so far this year without taking action. When the U.S. dollar passed 1.70 marks, comments briefly came from members of the Bundesbank Council to the effect that the deutschemark's revaluation of 1994 and 1995 had thus been corrected.

Ultimately, no serious efforts were made to stop the ascent of the U.S. dollar. Even when the psychologically-important level of 1.80 marks was tested last week, representatives of the Bundesbank council did not regard this development as worrisome. Comments reflecting a similar attitude also came from the federal government.
Nevertheless, the Bundesbank will probably try to effect a small correction by talking the dollar down in the next few weeks. This is not likely to stop the rise of the dollar permanently, however.
As long as the market regards an on-schedule start of EMU with a large number of participants as quite likeIy, the weakness of the mark will continue.
Despite assertions on the German side, a less rigid interpretation of the convergence criteria is already largely discounted by current rates.
Besides the debate surrounding the euro, however, the positive growth and interest rate gap between the United States and Germany also argues in favour of the U.S. dollar.
In addition, there is the remarkable improvement of the U.S. budget deficit. After about $300 billion at the beginning of the 199Os, it will probabIy fall to $45 billion this year.

The goal of balancing the budget is thus moving ever nearer. After testing the important technical resistance level at 1.80 marks, the six-year high of DM 1.8430 should be the next exchange rate target.

Rates of 1.85-1.90 marks should then move into the realm of concrete possibility in the next few weeks. Against this background, the mark would have thus lost about 23 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar within 12 months.

The dollar would then significantly surpass its "fair" exchange rate of about 1.73 marks based on purchasing power parity. The rising U.S. trade balance deficit could also burden the dollar in the medium term.

Of course, the mark's devaluation against the dollar constitutes a serious problem for German price stability and hence for the Bundesbank. Germany has an import ratio of about 27 percent relative to GDP.
In volume terms, the dollar sphere (USA, Canada, Australia) only accounts for 8.1 percent of total imports. 57.9 percent of German imports come from the EU.

The dollar has a much greater influence on import prices, however. Above all, raw materials (e.g. oil) are invoiced in US dollars and become more expensive immediately after a rise of the dollar rate.

The Bundesbank thus expects an increase in import prices by 3-4 percent on a revaluation of the U.S. dollar by 10 percent. Taking into consideration the mark's loss of value, we therefore expect a rise of German import prices by 3.7 percent to their highest level since 1989.

Nevertheless, the adverse effects of higher import prices on the German cost of living can be more than offset for the foreseeable future. For one thing, unit labour costs in the German industrial sector fell by more than 5 percent in the first four months of this year.

For another, the still relatively weak economic trend allows little manoeuvring room for passing on cost increases in higher prices. Producer prices have risen but only due to base effects. In the building sector price increases are also not feasible because of the prevailing industry recession.
The dangers on the inflation front thus remain small. We expect an inflation rate of 1.6 percent this year and of 2.0 percent in 1998.

A continuation of the mark's weakness in the near term may not be ruled out, especially since a weak mark is being politically tolerated to solve economic problems. Monetary and fiscal policy will not be further sources of stimulation, and structural changes (e.g. reducing sick pay) and tax reform will fail to get off the ground.
Export business will thus remain the mainstay of growth. In an environment of moderate growth and calm inflation, there is no reason for a change of monetary policy.

On a sustained increase of the dollar to values of 1.84-1.86 marks, the Bundesbank may decide to raise the repo rate slightly as a dampening measure or to switch to offering interest-rate-linked tenders. Though frequently discussed, such a switch could prove counterproductive.

In the short term, interest rates would probably rise, but the upward trend of the dollar is not likely to be stopped permanently by a small interest rate increase. Moreover, such a step would arouse negative sentiment in some European countries (e.g. France) ahead of the "Maastricht exam". The Bundesbank will therefore probably stick to offering volume-linked tenders at 3.0 percent in the near term.

Only in the coming year is the Bundesbank likely to step gently on the monetary brakes for domestic economic reasons. A somewhat brighter economic climate could be taken as a first opportunity to pass on cost increases in higher prices. After the rise of import prices, price relief from the domestic side would also abate. A small increase of the discount rate could then be expected in the second quarter of 1998 at the earliest. //The opinions expressed in this column represent those of the author only. They should not be seen as representing the view of Reuters.
